title: The solution report, from the records
request: Write the solution report a person or the main product can read: the problem, what the data shows, the decisions and why, results with intervals, limits and next steps, with every number taken from a record and no claim of production readiness.
spec: dclab_core.report: a SolutionReport and its rendering (Markdown, HTML, PDF) with the problem, findings, decisions, results with intervals, limits, next steps and a deliverables map when a rubric exists; every number from a record; the prose through the citation check. Done when each replica project's report renders, every number is traced to a record by a test, and no sentence calls a model production-ready.
plan: Built in an isolated worktree by a sub-agent: build() writes the report from the brief, findings, plan and stage records; numbers enter only through record paths.
Render Markdown and HTML purely; import reportlab only inside to_pdf (an optional extra), so the core keeps its four dependencies.
Write the studio adapter and trace every number of the three replica reports in tests.
Two dclab-reviewer passes; fix all 11 distinct findings with tests; merge into main.

decisions.decision: The prose is written by code, never a model; a line is kept only when every number in it traces to a record path.
decisions.why: A report for a reader or a grader must not invent or round away a number.

decisions.decision: The core has its own citation check rather than importing dclab_rnd/cited.py, with the same readiness rules.
decisions.why: The core may not import the studio.

decisions.decision: Odd record shapes cost a line, never the report, and a section that fails is named in the limits.
decisions.why: A report that crashes on a broken record says nothing; one that says what is missing is useful.

decisions.decision: The PDF is an optional extra imported only inside its function.
decisions.why: reportlab is not one of the core's four dependencies.

change: dclab_core/report.py (build with numbers mapped to record paths, check, Markdown, HTML, PDF), dclab_rnd/studio/solution_report.py, the pdf extra in the core's pyproject, a boundary test allowing reportlab only inside to_pdf; tests/test_core_report.py.

findings.defect: The report said the holdout was used once when the record said otherwise.
findings.scenario: A final record with holdout_uses_in_this_project 3 produced 'used once' in Results and 'scored 3 times' in Limits of the same report.
findings.cause: The Results sentence was fixed text, while the engine adds one to holdout_uses_in_this_project on every re-run of the final stage.
findings.fix: Write 'used once' only when the record says 1; otherwise the number of uses, traced, and the limits say the score is optimistic.
findings.impact: A project whose final stage was re-run would give its reader a report that says 'used once' in Results and 'scored 3 times' in Limits; anyone reading only Results would take an optimistic holdout score for a clean one.

findings.defect: Broken nested record shapes crashed build.
findings.scenario: A data record with evidence None, a final record with labels None, a decision given as a string, baselines or holdout metrics as lists, a review as a string: each raised AttributeError or TypeError.
findings.fix: Helpers that read any non-mapping as empty and any non-sequence as none, at every depth; the primary metric coerced to text.
findings.impact: One malformed nested field in any stage record, a None or a string where a mapping belongs, would stop the whole report from being built, so the person gets no report rather than one that names what is missing.

findings.defect: The overclaim rule was narrower than cited.py's, which it claimed to copy.
findings.scenario: A record limit 'The model is ready to deploy.' passed; so did production-grade, deployment-ready, safe to deploy, go live and production_ready with an underscore.
findings.fix: Copy cited.py's readiness and deployment phrases, fold underscores into separators; strict, a denial does not excuse it.
findings.impact: A record limit or note saying 'ready to deploy' or 'safe for production' would be printed in a report meant for a grader or the main product, while the report's own check passed it; the rule that benchmark evidence never claims readiness would hold only for one spelling.
alternatives: Import cited.py's rule instead of copying it: not possible, because dclab_core may not import dclab_rnd.

findings.defect: The title was never filtered or escaped.
findings.scenario: A project named 'Production-ready churn model' became the report's heading and the report failed its own check; a name with HTML or a newline reached report.md raw; the traced title differed from the written one.
findings.cause: The title bypassed the line rules.
findings.fix: Render, clip and escape the title as one line, trace its numbers, and replace it when it over-claims.
findings.impact: A project named 'Production-ready churn model' would get a report whose heading breaks the readiness rule and fails its own check, and a project name holding HTML or a newline would inject raw markup or a fake heading into report.md.

findings.defect: The deliverables map claimed coverage on a keyword match.
findings.scenario: A regression run with the rubric line 'Report precision and recall at the alert budget' was marked covered with no such line; 'on the test set' was mapped outside the report as tests; 'customer service tickets' as a service.
findings.cause: Single-word matching, and 'covered' whenever the stage record existed.
findings.fix: Match phrases (unit tests, a REST API, source control, a notebook are outside a report; the test set is not tests); a requirement is covered only when a kept line was written from its record, otherwise the map says where to look.
findings.impact: A grader reading the deliverables map would see 'covered' next to precision and recall at the alert budget on a regression run that wrote no such line, and requirements about the test set marked as outside the report, so the map misstates what was delivered.
alternatives: Write 'see <section>' for every matched requirement, the reviewer's smallest option: it would never claim coverage, but it would also never confirm a requirement the report does meet; coverage tied to a kept line from the requirement's record does both.

findings.defect: Clipping could cut inside a number, and the report then failed its own check.
findings.scenario: A model name ending in a 200-digit run was cut mid-token; the report printed a truncated number that matched no record.
findings.cause: The clip had no notion of tokens.
findings.fix: Never cut inside a number, and run the check again on the finished sections.
findings.impact: A long model or parameter name ending in digits would be cut mid-number, so the report printed a number no record holds and then failed check(), which a host calls before showing the report.

findings.defect: Some text entered a line without tracing.
findings.scenario: Decision status and source were rendered plainly, and an unknown metric name such as ndcg@10 was written raw; with a tolerance on integers a number could be attributed to the wrong path.
findings.cause: Not every field went through the tracing writer.
findings.fix: Trace status, source and unknown metric names like any record text.
findings.impact: A number inside an untraced status or metric name could be matched, through the tolerance on integers, to a different record path, so a reader following the trace would land on the wrong value.

findings.defect: Some numbers were invisible to the tracer, and one was changed.
findings.scenario: Record text 'threshold .5 kept' passed the check because a leading-dot decimal was not a number; NFKC normalisation turned a record's '10²' into '102'.
findings.cause: The number pattern and the text normalisation.
findings.fix: Leading-dot decimals are numbers; text is normalised with NFC, not NFKC.
findings.impact: A record's '.5' entered the report with no trace and no check, and '10²' was printed as '102', a value the record never held, in a report whose whole promise is that every number traces.

findings.defect: The report described a bootstrap interval that never ran.
findings.scenario: When every draw failed the runner returned low = high = point with 0 draws, and the report still wrote the interval as the range the score could take.
findings.cause: The draws count was not read.
findings.fix: Write an interval only when its bootstrap drew resamples.
findings.impact: When every bootstrap draw failed, the report would present a zero-width interval as the range the holdout score could take, telling the reader the score was certain when nothing had been resampled.

findings.scenario: reportlab was installed nowhere, so every PDF assertion was skipped, while the playbook row said all three formats render.
findings.cause: An optional dependency absent from the test environment.
findings.fix: Install reportlab in the main environment so the PDF tests run (skipped where it is missing); reportlab is still not in requirements/base.txt, recorded as open.
findings.impact: The PDF, one of the three formats the package claims, could have been broken with every test green, because each PDF assertion was skipped where reportlab was missing.
findings.open: reportlab is still not in requirements/base.txt, so the PDF tests skip on any environment where it was not installed by hand.

findings.defect: The findings shown were read on rows that include most of the holdout, and the report did not say so.
findings.scenario: The adapter re-ran the analysis on a seeded 80% of the whole table, which overlaps the run's grouped holdout; the core hard-coded a sentence calling these rows 'before the holdout'.
findings.cause: The adapter did not rebuild the run's split.
findings.fix: Read the findings on the run's own training rows (rebuilt through engine.prepare, at most 20,000 rows); when the split cannot be rebuilt, fall back to the plan's rows and say they include most held-out rows; the host passes the sentence.
findings.impact: 'What the data shows' related columns to the target partly on rows the run had held out, under a sentence calling them pre-holdout rows, so a reader would take holdout-informed figures for training-only ones; no model used them, but the report's honesty claim was false.
alternatives: Only reword the sentence to say the rows include most of the holdout, the reviewer's first option: kept as the fallback when the split cannot be rebuilt, because reading the run's own training rows removes the overlap instead of disclosing it.
findings.open: When the run's split cannot be rebuilt, the findings are still read on the plan's rows, which include most held-out rows; the report says so instead of avoiding it.

measurements.name: traced reports of the replica projects
measurements.gate: Each replica project's report renders, every number in it is traced to a record, and no sentence calls a model production-ready (Done-when of 17.7).
measurements.result: The fraud (label-file flow), ticket and delivery-time projects run end to end; every number in each Markdown is parsed and traced to a record value, every digit is a traced number or part of a name; Markdown, HTML and PDF render (reportlab 4.4.5).
measurements.against_gate: Every number in each replica's Markdown (fraud through its label-file flow, tickets, delivery time) was parsed and traced to a record value, and every digit is a traced number or part of a name, which meets 'every number traced'. Markdown, HTML and PDF render, the PDF with reportlab 4.4.5, which meets 'renders'. The numbers given do not restate the readiness clause; the replica tests assert that no sentence makes such a claim.
limits: Tracing shows each number came from a record, not that the record is right or that the sentence around it reads the record correctly.
The test traces with the same number pattern as the code, so a number form neither recognises (as leading-dot decimals were before the review) passes both.
Only replica projects built from invented data were traced end to end; odd real-record shapes are covered by unit tests of shapes, not by a traced report.
The review fixes were committed without a further review of their own.

outcome: Done: a SolutionReport built from the records, every number traced to its path, no readiness claim, robust to any record shape, in Markdown, HTML and PDF; 11 findings from two reviews fixed. Open: no route, page or intern tool shows it yet; reportlab is not in the base requirements; model-written prose is 18.7.
lessons: A report must derive even its connective claims ('used once') from the records, or it contradicts itself.
Copy a safety rule completely, or reference it; a narrower copy gives a false sense of coverage.
Unicode compatibility normalisation can change numbers; use NFC for text that carries figures.
A test that is skipped where the dependency is missing proves nothing there; install it where the claim is made.
risks: Connective text such as 'used once', 'covered' or 'the range the score could take' can contradict the records even when every number traces.
A copied safety rule (the readiness phrases of cited.py) can drift narrower than its source and give false coverage.
Normalising, clipping or a narrow number pattern can change or hide a number between the record and the page.
Real records come in odd shapes; a report that crashes on one leaves the reader with nothing.
Findings shown in the report may be read on rows that overlap the run's holdout unless the run's split is rebuilt.
